title: a year of service designed
hook: Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Krishna agrees
carry: a loose hand on the results

segments.voice: Yesterday, a year of service designed, piece four: the guest, atithi devo bhava. Is there a name on your calendar now, someone to invite in? Day nine hundred seventy-three.
screen: `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA.` · `ONE NAME ON THE CALENDAR.`

segments.voice: Plans made in a quiet week have a way of dissolving once the busy weeks come back. Arjuna knew the problem from the inside. In chapter six of the Gita, Krishna has been describing a mind that rests even and steady, and Arjuna pushes back. The mind, he says, is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Holding it still seems to me as hard as holding the wind. It's a very human moment, a student saying, that sounds lovely, but I don't think I can. What's striking is that Krishna doesn't argue. Today, at the week's end, the piece of the design that keeps the rest alive.
screen: `PLANS DISSOLVE IN BUSY WEEKS.` → `AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA DOESN'T ARGUE.`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer, in paraphrase: no doubt, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held by abhyasa and vairagya. Abhyasa is practice, the same thing done again and again. Vairagya is letting go, loosening the grip of wanting. That's it. No secret technique. Just practice, and a looser hand. Now look back over this week through that pair. We began with karma. In chapter five, the true renouncer is the one who neither hates nor craves, and the lotus leaf sits in the water all day without getting wet. That's vairagya: staying in the work, letting the results roll off. Then we started designing a year of service. Delight in the good of all beings gave the reason. Svadharma gave the where: your own service, done imperfectly. The gift gave four questions: why, what back, when, to whom. The guest gave the door. All of that is a design. What it still needs is abhyasa. A year of service isn't one big decision. It's a rhythm. One day a week, one evening a month, one gift each season, one meal shared when the calendar comes round. Abhyasa, on this reading, is more about returning than about intensity. And vairagya keeps the rhythm from turning into a tally of hits and misses, because the day you miss, or the gift that goes unthanked, is just water on the leaf. Arjuna said the mind was like the wind. Krishna didn't say it wasn't. He said there's a way to hold it, and it looks a lot like showing up again.
screen: `ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA.` · `THIS WEEK: THE LEAF, ALL BEINGS, THE GIFT, THE GUEST.` · `A YEAR OF SERVICE IS A RHYTHM.` · `A MISSED DAY IS WATER ON THE LEAF.` · then, large: `SHOW UP AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest the hands. Let the breath be the practice: in, out, again. When the mind runs off, and it will, notice where it went, and come back without scolding. That's abhyasa and vairagya in miniature: returning, and not gripping. As you sit, let this week's pieces come up one at a time, the leaf, the good of all beings, your own service, the gift, the guest, and for each, ask one question: how often? Weekly, monthly, once a season? Let a rhythm suggest itself. If you pray, you can offer that rhythm to the one you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Abhyasa. Practice that repeats, held together with vairagya, a loose hand on the results.
Your line: a loose hand on the results. Today, give one piece of your design a rhythm, weekly, monthly or seasonal, and write it where you'll see it. Day nine hundred seventy-three.

screen: `DAY 973 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.`

howItsDone: Some Hindus keep service in a regular rhythm, such as a weekly shift in a temple kitchen or giving tied to festivals in the calendar, and teachers point to the Gita's pairing of abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go, for steadying the mind.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: abhyasa, practice, paired with vairagya in Gita 6.35.

trapdoor: what you thought: a year of service is one big decision.
what it means: in the Gita's terms it's abhyasa, a rhythm repeated, with vairagya, a loose hand on how it turns out.
what a scholar hears: Gita 6.34–35, Arjuna's wind and Krishna's pairing of abhyasa and vairagya, a pairing the Yoga Sutras also make.
